Most people do not have a LinkedIn problem.

They have a finishing problem.

They draft a sharp post, then rewrite it until it sounds like a keynote, then never hit publish.

The accounts that grow are usually not the cleverest. They are the ones that show up on a schedule with one useful idea, written the way they talk at work.

If you are waiting for a perfect week of content, you will still be waiting next quarter.

What is the post you have been sitting on?

Every other request we get is "just write a small custom module."

It is rarely small. We are the ones who have to upgrade it, explain it to the next consultant, and own it when Odoo moves a field in 19.0.

Last month a customer wanted a unique inventory workflow. The instinct on their side was development. Ours was: sit on our hands for a day and try the stock of settings first. A few configuration tweaks covered it. No extra module. No extra bill of materials for our maintenance calendar.

I would rather lose a customisation invoice than inherit a fork we cannot stand behind after the next upgrade.

We still write modules. We ship them when configuration actually cannot carry the process. The filter is simple: will we still be proud of this code after two version jumps?

When do you push back on a customisation that looks easy on paper?

#Configuration #Customization #Odoo #Inventory

I will not put an AI feature on one of our Odoo apps until I have seen the master data.

We tried anyway once. Invoice approvals, discrepancy flags, the whole demo-friendly stack. On paper it looked like we had a product. In production the vendor names disagreed with themselves, amounts had typos, and the model spent its intelligence shouting about duplicates that were just dirty records.

Our team spent more hours cleaning data than the assistant ever saved. That is on me. I shipped clever before I shipped boring.

Now the rule inside the company is blunt: clean the partners, products, and taxes first. Then we talk about models. A workflow that looks smart on top of a mess just scales the mess.

What is the first table you would refuse to automate until it is clean?

#AI #DataQuality #MasterData #Invoices

The AI invoice demo always looks finished. Vendor PDF in, Odoo bill out.

We built that path. Scan, extract, write the vendor bill. Then the real inbox showed up: twenty vendor layouts, half of them scans, a few with the tax in a footnote. The model filled fields. Our accountants spent the afternoon unscrewing them.

I stopped treating extraction as the product. The product is what we allow to hit posted data.

Now we only let AI draft. A person still owns the confirm. And we spend the money on vendor templates and master data before we spend it on another model.

I would rather ship a slower, trusted bill than a fast one we have to reverse on month-end.

Where do you still require a human confirm before anything writes into Odoo?

#AI #Invoices #DocumentAI #Automation

We treated a payment-gateway integration as a weekend job.

Collect the payment. Write the accounting. Happy path in the sandbox. Then live traffic arrived: paid in the gateway, not paid in Odoo, or the reverse. We owned both sides of that lie in front of the customer.

The bug was not the API. It was that "success" did not mean the same thing in both systems. Statuses, retries, partial captures — none of that was in the sales conversation.

We stopped, mapped every state, and wrote the boring document nobody wanted. That mapping is now the first artefact I ask for before we take an integration onto our plate.

I will not sell "it just syncs" again. If we cannot name the failure states, we are not ready to ship.

What status mismatch have you had to explain to a customer after go-live?

#Integrations #Payments #Odoo #Accounting

Migrations are critical, but they’re not as straightforward as they seem. I always start with the data. I check for completeness, accuracy, and any discrepancies that could lead to havoc post-migration.

Recently, we had a client who wanted to migrate from an outdated system to Odoo. The initial assessment looked promising — they showed us their database and it seemed tidy. We discovered later, during a deeper dive, that their SKU numbers were not standardized. Some were numeric, others alphanumeric, and it got worse with product categories.

If we had moved forward without addressing these issues, the migration would have failed. Products would be mismatched, inventory levels could be incorrect, and financial reporting would spiral into chaos. This taught us a lesson: don't just trust initial data presentations. Dig deeper to reveal hidden complexities.

What’s your go-to check before a migration? Any surprises you've encountered that changed your approach?

#Migration #Odoo #Inventory

We've all seen AI that drafts content. It's great for generating ideas or creating templates, but there's a hard line when it comes to allowing it to write directly into production data. Recently, we faced a scenario where a customer wanted to automate responses to support tickets using AI. The drafting AI could produce coherent replies, but when we considered letting it post directly to the ticketing system, I pushed back.

Here’s why: drafting doesn’t account for the nuances of each ticket. An AI can misinterpret context or misapply tone. It might suggest a resolution that doesn't fit due to missing background knowledge. I insisted we keep a manual review step before any AI-generated reply hit the system.

In this case, it was about risk management. The stakes are high when a customer is relying on us for accurate and consistent communication. Automating too freely can lead to errors that damage trust.

Are you letting your AI write directly into production, or do you have a review process? What’s your experience?

#AI #Automation #SupportOps #ERP

When I have to explain a technical decision to a non-technical operations owner, it’s a balancing act. I often find that my choice of words matters more than the logic behind the decision itself.

Last week, I pushed back on implementing a seemingly simple customization. The request was straightforward: change how a report looks. But the implications were anything but simple. Modifying that report would affect data integrity across the system. It could lead to confusion in downstream processes, especially if the same data was referenced elsewhere.

I had to explain that while the change would solve an immediate need, it could create a ripple effect in our data structure. That’s when I lean into analogies that relate to their daily operations. I likened it to changing a traffic signal at a busy intersection. It might ease one flow of traffic but could lead to chaos elsewhere.

By framing the decision in a context they understand, I was able to get their buy-in. It turned out to be a valuable lesson: clarity in communication is as crucial as the technical decision itself.

How do you approach explaining complex technical decisions to your operations team?

#Customization #Odoo

One of the most common missteps in Odoo implementations is rushing to install a module. There’s often a temptation to grab the shiny new tool without fully understanding the implications.

I recently had a client who insisted on installing a popular inventory management module. It looked promising on the surface. But once it was live, we hit a wall. The module wasn’t compatible with their existing workflows. Features that were supposed to streamline operations ended up creating additional complexity.

We spent more time fixing the fallout than if we had taken a moment to assess their unique needs. The team ended up frustrated, and the initial excitement was replaced with confusion.

Before installing any module, I now recommend a rigorous evaluation against actual business processes. It’s critical to ensure that what looks good on paper will truly deliver value in practice.

How do you evaluate new modules before installation?

#Inventory #Odoo

User adoption often gets overlooked in ERP implementations. We focus on the shiny features, the integrations, and the AI capabilities, but the real risk lurks in how users interact with the system.

I’ve seen projects fail not because of technical issues, but because the team didn’t embrace the system. They didn’t understand why certain workflows mattered or how to leverage the new tools.

Take a recent implementation of an Odoo CRM module. We spent weeks customizing it, integrating it with existing systems, and testing every feature. But during training, I realized many users were still attached to their old processes.

They needed to see the value in using the new system — not just in theory, but in real, tangible outcomes. That’s when I knew we had to pivot our strategy. We began focusing on hands-on training and involving users in the customization process.

Now, when we roll out a new feature, it’s not just a demo. It’s about making sure every user feels like they are part of the journey. Without that buy-in, no amount of technology will succeed.

How do you ensure your users adopt the systems you implement?

#Customization #Integrations #AI #ERP

RAG assistants can be helpful, but they can also hallucinate. When using them over company documents, the value often depends on the quality of the underlying data. Recently, we had a case where a client used an AI assistant to pull insights from their product documentation. The assistant generated some useful summaries but also presented incorrect details that led to confusion in a meeting.

The challenge was that the documents had inconsistencies, and the assistant filled in gaps with assumptions. This is where RAG can mislead teams that rely on it without validating the output.

In contrast, when the same assistant is trained on clean, structured data, it can lead to actionable insights. It’s about understanding the boundaries of AI assistance and knowing when to validate or question the output. We need to remind ourselves that AI is a tool, not a replacement for critical thinking and domain knowledge. How do you keep your data clean and ensure your AI outputs remain reliable?

#AI #DataQuality

In manufacturing, the balance between customization and standardization can make or break an implementation. I remember a project where a client insisted on tailoring every aspect of their production module. They wanted unique workflows, custom reports, and specific alerts for each machine. It seemed reasonable at first. But as we dove deeper, it became clear that this level of customization would lead to complexity, especially with Odoo’s updates and maintenance.

We pushed back, advocating for a more standardized approach with minor tweaks that would still meet their operational needs. The argument was simple: a complex setup means higher risks during upgrades and a steeper learning curve for users. Their team needed to focus on production efficiency, not wrestling with a labyrinthine system.

In the end, we agreed on a middle ground—customizations that added value without losing sight of usability. Now, the system is robust and flexible enough to adapt as their operations evolve without losing stability.

Have you faced a similar dilemma between customization and standardization in your implementations?

#Customization #Manufacturing #Odoo

I’ve seen automation projects that seemed like a smart move but ended up complicating simple tasks. A couple of months ago, a client wanted to automate their invoice approval process. The idea was to streamline operations and reduce manual handling.

But here’s the catch: automating approvals meant that the system would bypass a critical review step that had been working just fine as a checklist. The team was used to a human touch in validating invoices against delivery notes and past interactions.

Once the automation went live, we quickly faced issues. Invoices slipped through that shouldn’t have, leading to disputes and delays with vendors. What looked like efficiency turned into chaos.

Now we’re rolling back parts of that automation to reintroduce manual checks. Sometimes, keeping it simple is the best approach. Not every process needs to be automated. Sometimes a checklist can do the job better than an AI.

What tasks do you think should remain manual despite the push for automation?

Debugging an Odoo issue that only surfaces in production can be a real test of patience and skill. I recently faced this exact situation. The system was running smoothly in our staging environment, yet, come Monday morning, users reported a critical error with invoicing.

We had to investigate quickly. The first step was to replicate the issue. I gathered logs and attempted to reproduce the error under the same conditions as the production setup. No luck.

Next, I turned to the environment specifics. Was there a difference in data? Was there a race condition that didn’t appear in staging? After digging into the user reports, I discovered that a specific combination of user roles and permissions was triggering the bug. It was an oversight during the initial configuration that slipped through the testing phase.

The lesson here is clear: production environments can behave differently than testing. Always consider real-world scenarios and edge cases when you’re validating your system. What steps do you take when an issue only arises in production?

Many AI copilot demos look impressive but fall flat in real-world applications. For a warehouse or finance team, the difference is in practical usability.

In one project, we tested an AI copilot that claimed to assist with inventory management. The demo showcased its ability to analyze data and provide insight. However, in reality, it struggled with the specific terminology and workflows our team used. Instead of enhancing productivity, it added confusion.

In contrast, a tailored AI solution that understood our operations and integrated seamlessly into existing workflows proved invaluable. It allowed the team to pull reports with relevant metrics without needing extensive training. The key was ensuring the AI was designed for the users, not just the demo room.

Next time you evaluate an AI copilot, ask: Will it genuinely fit into the workflow, or is it just a flashy feature?

Dirty master data undermines even the best AI workflows. I encountered this in a recent project where a client was eager to implement an AI-driven invoice processing tool. They focused on the glitzy features, confident it would solve their problems with efficiency and accuracy. But when we dived into the data, we uncovered inconsistencies that would derail the entire operation. Vendor names were misspelled, invoice formats varied wildly, and duplicate entries were rampant. The AI assistant, while sophisticated, couldn't compensate for this chaos.

After several frustrating attempts to integrate the AI tool, we pivoted back to the basics: cleaning the master data. It was a tedious process, but it became clear that without this foundational step, we would only be automating errors. This experience reinforced the importance of rigorous data quality checks before deploying any AI solution in an ERP context. It’s a reminder that clever tech is only as good as the data it’s fed.

How do you ensure data quality before launching an AI project?

We recently tackled a seemingly minor Odoo customization for a client. They needed a simple change in their sales order workflow, just a field modification to streamline data entry. It appeared straightforward. But as we dug deeper, the implications unfolded.

Adjusting the sales order structure meant re-evaluating dependencies across multiple modules. Integrations with inventory and accounting systems were affected. Small changes can trigger a cascade of unforeseen challenges within your ERP.

Every customization, no matter how trivial it seems, deserves thorough analysis. It’s not about the immediate request; it’s about understanding the underlying architecture and how every piece fits together.

Choosing between configuring Odoo and developing a custom module can be tricky. I've faced this dilemma multiple times during implementations. A few months back, a client wanted very specific functionality that was not available out of the box. They asked for a custom module to handle unique inventory tracking requirements.

At first glance, it seemed necessary. But after digging into their request, we found that many of their needs could be met by proper configuration of existing modules. By using Odoo's built-in features, we could save them time and money while ensuring easier future upgrades. Custom modules can lead to technical debt and maintenance challenges.

The right approach often depends on the underlying business processes. If the requirement is common across industries, configuration typically works best. Custom modules should be reserved for unique cases where no alternative exists.

In the end, we opted for configuration, which not only addressed the client's needs but also left them with a cleaner system. Have you faced a similar situation where a potential custom build turned out to be better served by configuration?

Dirty master data undermines even the best AI workflows. I encountered this in a recent project where a client wanted to implement an AI-driven invoice processing tool. They were captivated by the promise of efficiency and accuracy. But we had to pull back.

Before we even considered deploying the AI, we did a thorough review of their data. It was a mess—duplicate vendors, inconsistent product names, and missing values. We spent weeks cleaning it up.

This wasn't just a checklist item. It was essential. The AI tool would only be as good as the data feeding it. If the foundation is shaky, the results will be too.

The lesson? Effective AI deployment in ERP relies more on the quality of your master data than on the sophistication of the technology itself. What’s your experience with data quality impacting AI implementations?

I've seen AI solutions pitched as the answer to every operational headache. Recently, a client insisted on using AI to handle their invoice processing. They envisioned a seamless flow from receipt to approval with little human intervention.

The reality? AI can process data, but it can't interpret context. Their invoices came with various formats, line items, and nuances that were unique to each vendor. The AI struggled. Instead of reducing workload, we found ourselves spending more time training the system on edge cases and exceptions.

We had to pause. The most effective solution ended up being a mixture of manual oversight and AI assistance. The team still needed to validate outputs, ensuring accuracy. In the end, we struck a balance between automation and human judgment.

AI is a tool, not a silver bullet. It requires careful integration into existing workflows, especially where human discretion is critical.

How do you decide when AI is the right fit for your operational challenges?

Recent discussions about LLMs often spotlight the promise of AI copilots in various sectors. While the idea of automating parts of finance and warehouse operations sounds appealing, I've learned to be cautious. Copilots must enhance human expertise, not replace it.

In my experience, attempting to automate complex support tasks can lead to more complications than it solves. A finance team may trust a copilot to draft a report, but without a keen human eye, essential context could be missed. Misinterpretations can easily propagate through operations when decisions are based on AI outputs without oversight.

We regularly deal with clients who want to streamline processes. However, I've firmly pushed back against automating functions like vendor communications or financial reconciliations. The nuances in these tasks demand human judgment. If an AI copilot can't do more than fill in blanks, it shouldn't be in the driver's seat.

A human touch in operations isn’t just a preference; it’s necessary for accuracy and trust. What’s your experience with balancing automation and human oversight?

A recent spike in chatter about open-source AI agents has raised eyebrows. Tools like Allos and OpenClaw promise rapid deployment and flexibility. Sounds exciting. But here's the catch: excitement doesn't always translate to production readiness.

As a practitioner, I see too many teams excited about shiny new models without considering their operational landscape. A model drop may look impressive in demos, but integrating it into existing workflows? Entirely different game. We’ve had cases where a new LLM caused more headaches than solutions, especially with messy master data.

When evaluating a new model, I focus on three core questions:
What data will it work with?
How will it integrate with current systems?
And most importantly, will it really improve our performance?

Without answers, we risk chasing noise rather than value. Let’s invest our time in tools that enhance the existing operations, not create new problems.

What new AI model caught your interest, and did it deliver in practice?

There's a lot of buzz around new open-source AI tools like Allos and EZClaw. They promise quick deployment and flexibility, which is attractive. But excitement doesn’t mean they’re ready for production.

I prioritize three gates before releasing any AI feature.

First, cost. I assess the infrastructure and integration expenses. If the AI tool isn’t cost-effective, we’ll burn resources fast. Then, latency. If an AI feature can’t keep up with real-time demands, it’s a hard pass. Users expect seamless experiences, not lagging processes. Lastly, trust. I won’t ship anything unless I’m confident in its accuracy and reliability. Misinformation in production can ruin workflows and erode user faith in the system.

These gates aren’t just checkboxes; they ensure that when we push something out, it’s not just functional but also dependable.

How do you ensure readiness in your AI deployments?

The recent wave of open-source AI tools like Allos and EZClaw has stirred excitement. They promise easy deployment of AI agents, but I see a need for caution.

On the surface, these tools appear to streamline processes, making it easier to connect AI agents with Odoo/ERP APIs. However, many fail to account for the messy realities of production. Last week, we had a project where a new tool-calling agent looked promising in theory. It handled initial requests without issue, but when we tested it with real data, the breakdowns began.

Misconfigured endpoints. Data mismatches. Unforeseen latency issues. Each error revealed gaps that weren’t visible in the sandbox. The excitement of rapid deployment faded quickly when we saw the operational hurdles.

Before I trust any new integration, I interrogate the failure modes that matter. What happens when the data isn't clean? What are the limits of error handling?

It reminds me that not every shiny tool will survive the demands of a live environment. What challenges have you faced with new AI tools in production?

Document AI is often hailed for its transformative potential, but its real-world application can be challenging. Just last week, I encountered a situation where a customer needed to automate invoice processing. Their invoices were a mix of scanned documents with varying formats, stamps, and multiple languages. Sounds simple, right?

Not quite. In this case, our existing Document AI struggled with the messy inputs. The OCR accuracy dropped significantly due to inconsistent formatting and language shifts. We had to take a step back and enhance our pre-processing workflows.

Instead of just throwing an advanced model at the problem, we refined our approach to handle the different document types they were using. We focused on improving data extraction, ensuring that we had not just a faster solution, but one that was reliable enough to prevent errors in financial reporting.

It’s a clear reminder that AI must fit the realities of business operations. If it can’t handle the messiness of real-world data, it isn't worth implementing.

How have you tackled similar challenges in your own AI projects?

In warehouses, the stakes are high. We can’t afford a system that works well in a controlled environment but fails when real data and real tasks come into play. A demo AI copilot might look impressive, but if it can’t handle messy inputs—like inconsistent item descriptions or unexpected inventory anomalies—it won’t earn trust from the team on the ground.

I refuse to ship AI solutions that haven’t gone through rigorous testing under actual operational stress. For instance, we recently piloted an AI copilot for inventory management. It performed flawlessly on demo data but stumbled when tackling our clients' diverse SKU formats.

The key takeaway? A copilot must be tailored to the specific challenges faced in production, not just the flashy features that shine in demos. How do you ensure your AI tools bridge the gap between demo and deployment?
